title: New Designs of Multivariate-Polynomial Universal Hash Functions
authors: Jean Paul Degabriele, Jan Gilcher, Jérôme Govinden, and Kenneth G. Paterson
abstract: Universal hash functions (UHFs) are basic building blocks in cryptography, making the topic of designing secure, fast UHFs of longstanding interest. This paper presents an exploration of the design space for multivariate UHFs, that is UHFs that involve the evaluation of a multivariate polynomial over a finite field. We focus on two-level designs, wherein a lower-level hash function produces intermediate values that are consumed by a higher-level one, and where both hash functions are based on either univariate or multivariate polynomials. This approach allows designs to benefit from the desirable features of both components and thereby strike new trade-offs between key size, security level, and amenability to optimization techniques. We extend the recent UHF code generation and benchmarking framework of Degabriele et al. (IEEE S&P 2024) to accommodate our multivariate designs (and also to support binary field arithmetic). We then use the framework to study the performance of a large collection of new two-level designs. This is done by first conducting a statistical factor analysis to determine which design features (and combinations of those features) most influence performance, and then using it to identify particular combinations of lower-level and higher-level hash functions offering particularly good performance/security trade-offs. We present new designs for both binary and prime fields, at two different security levels (corresponding to roughly 128 and 256 bits of security). Our best designs have performance that significantly outperforms state-of-the-art UHFs in the research literature and as deployed in mainstream cryptography libraries by up to 25%, resulting in 0.3 cycles/byte for 128-bit binary fields. We expect further gains from optimizations such as vectorization, as our benchmarks rely purely on auto-generated code from the extended framework, while state-of-the-art implementations typically use hand-optimized implementation strategies. We conclude with a brief inquiry into the performance implications of employing our best UHF design in the AEAD and Accordion mode designs currently under consideration for standardization by NIST.

1        Introduction
Universal hash functions (UHFs) are lightweight keyed hash functions satisfying a weak security notion.
Security is only guaranteed as long as the key and hash digests are hidden from the adversary. However,
their security is typically based on combinatorial techniques and thus holds even against computation-
ally unbounded adversaries. Today, UHFs constitute an essential component in symmetric cryptography.
Through the classical construction of Carter and Wegman they can be combined with a single block cipher
call to yield very fast MAC designs over variable-length messages [8]. Such MAC constructions can be
found in the two most widely deployed AEAD schemes today: GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, which use
the UHFs GHASH and Poly1305 respectively. UHFs are also found in several more advanced MAC and

AEAD designs. One notable case is in Accordion mode designs (variable-input-length tweakable ciphers),
which NIST is currently planning to standardize [30]. An Accordion mode can be easily morphed into an
AEAD scheme with the strongest possible security [21] or applied directly for disk encryption and other
applications requiring encryption without ciphertext expansion, also providing the best possible security.
Accordion mode constructions typically use two UHF instances and one encryption layer, e.g. AES-CTR,
as in the currently favored NIST candidate HCTR2 [30]. Thus, in Accordion constructions, UHFs are even
more crucial to the overall performance of the scheme.
    Given their prominent role in the design of practical and efficient encryption schemes, there has been
a substantial body of work proposing several optimized UHF designs. The vast majority rely on algebraic
structures over some finite field within the following three categories.

Classical Polynomial. The most popular construction is the classical (univariate) polynomial construc-
tion [12, 24, 35]. Both GHASH and Poly1305 use this design, where GHASH is a polynomial over a 128-bit
binary field and Poly1305 is a polynomial over the prime field corresponding to 2130 − 5. Here the message
is mapped to the polynomial coefficients, and the digest is computed evaluating the polynomial on the
secret key. Its benefits are that it is conceptually simple, requires very short keys (the size of a single field
element), supports online evaluation (using Horner’s rule), and is parallelizable [10].

(Pseudo) Inner Product. A less known alternative is the inner product construction, already pro-
posed by Carter and Wegman in 1979 [8] and later employed in the MMH construction by Halevi and
Krawczyk [20]. Here the message and key are treated as two equal-length vectors over a finite field and
the hash digest is their inner product. A related construction, also described in [8], is the pseudo inner
product construction behind the NMH design [20] and UMAC [26]. It uses a similar algebraic structure
but requires only half the number of multiplications as the inner product and classical polynomial. This
comes at the cost of an equal increase in the number of additions but, since multiplication is typically
more computationally intensive, it still results in significant speedups. The main limitation of MMH and
NMH is that they require a key as long as the message.

BRW Polynomial. UHF designs with large key sizes are not as practical as the overhead in generating
the key material often outweighs their performance gains. They also incur higher CPU cache consumption.
This motivated Bernstein to ask whether it was possible to combine the short key size of the classical
polynomial with the reduced multiplication complexity of the pseudo inner product construction. Building
on ideas by Rabin and Winograd, he proposed such a construction that came to be known as the Bernstein-
Rabin-Winograd (BRW) polynomial [3]. Although the BRW polynomial manages to combine the best
of both worlds, it also introduces new limitations. Unlike the prior two, no parallelizable algorithm is
known for evaluating the BRW polynomial. Furthermore, it is incompatible with popular field-arithmetic
optimization techniques, such as delayed limb realignment, delayed carry, and delayed reduction which
enable significant speedups in typical implementations [10].

A Unified View. Stepping back for a moment, we observe that, the classical polynomial, the pseudo
inner product, and the BRW polynomial, are all instances of multivariate polynomials. More specifically,
they represent edge-case instances with extreme traits in the full space of multivariate polynomials, e.g.,
single variable with full degree (classical polynomial) vs maximum number of variables with degree one
(inner product). On a more practical level, if we consider the following three goals, (a) short keys,
(b) reduced multiplication complexity, and (c) compatibility with delayed-operation optimizations and
parallelizability, we observe that each construction satisfies exactly two of these properties but not all
three. This poses the following research question:

 Can we identify new universal hash designs that strike better trade-offs and attain better performance?

    For instance, in ChaCha20-Poly1305, the key material for the hash is obtained via a separate call to
the ChaCha20 block function where currently only 16 bytes of the available 48 bytes are used. A UHF
design exploiting this free key material would clearly be beneficial in that setting. As existing designs
lie at the extremities in the space of multivariate polynomials, it is likely that UHF designs with more
balanced trade-offs can be found within the interior of this space. Accordingly, we set out to study and
systematically explore the space of multivariate-polynomials in order to improve the state of the art in
UHF design.
    Our search through the space of multivariate polynomials is of course not exhaustive. Instead, it
is informed by the current state of the art in UHF design and their optimized implementations. Our
exploration is based on a two-level hash structure composing two simpler polynomials from a carefully
selected set of candidates having unique and attractive features. When both components are multivariate
polynomials, the two-level structure will yield another multivariate polynomial. By employing this two-
level structure we obtain hybrid constructions that can benefit from the advantageous features of both
components. This allows us to strike different trade-offs between key size, security level, and amenability
to various optimizations that we cannot achieve using a single atomic polynomial. For example, we can
employ multiple instances of a highly efficient and parallelizable polynomial at the lower level, and combine
their outputs at the higher level with another polynomial that is less parallelizable but which yields a better
security bound with less key material. One immediate benefit of this two-level structure is that the key
material can be reused across the lower-level polynomial instances, thereby reducing the overall key size.
    This two-level structure was originally proposed to speed up implementations of classical polynomial
hash functions, by decomposing a classical polynomial into a combination of two classical polynomials
[23, 17, 10]. It was also used in two recent hash designs, Hash2L and d-2LHash, combining the BRW
polynomial with the classical polynomial [9, 5]. We explore this two-level structure more thoroughly
than prior work, considering several different candidates at each level and evaluating the security and
performance of each composition. We are interested in the security of each composition as an almost-∆-
universal hash function and its performance measured in the customary metric of cycles per byte. To assess
the performance of the different options, we build on the framework of Degabriele et al. [10], extending
its functionality to support our new constructions and using it to compare and contrast different design
choices. Through this approach we make several novel contributions, as explained below.

1.1   Our Contributions
Security of Multivariate Polynomials. We start by formally analyzing the security of multivariate
polynomial hash functions. Namely, we establish the almost-universality and almost-∆-universality of
multivariate polynomials over any finite field under an injectivity assumption and derive security bounds
in terms of the total degree of the multivariate polynomial. This result is stated in Thm. 4. Polynomial
hash functions satisfying the conditions of our theorem have the additional benefit of admitting variants
with fewer keys.

New Multivariate-Polynomial Hash Designs. Next, we identify suitable candidate polynomials to
insert at the lower and higher levels of the two-level hash construction. In such construction, most of
the computation happens at the lower level, and thus, an efficient choice of polynomial is crucial here.
We consider four distinct lower-level polynomials MMH+ , SQH+ , NMH+ , HKM, where the first three are
variants of prior works [20, 15] and HKM is a new design. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has
used these polynomials to instantiate the two-level construction. Each strikes a different trade-off between
parallelizability, support for delayed limb realignment, key size, and number of field arithmetic operations

needed. All require relatively large keys when compared to the alternative choice of BRW that is employed
in Hash2L and d-2LHash, but they are simpler to implement. Moreover, in the two-level construction, their
effective key size is significantly reduced due to the reuse of keys across instances.
    At the higher level, our focus shifts to optimizing the trade-off between the amount of key material and
obtaining a good security bound for long messages without degrading performance. Here we consider five
choices of polynomials: tMMH, tSQH, tNMH, t̂BRW, MHP. The first three are tree-based constructions
instantiated with MMH+ , SQH+ , and NMH+ respectively. The instantiations with SQH+ and NMH+
appear to be new. The remaining two constructions, t̂BRW and MHP, are novel multivariate generalizations
of BRW and the classical univariate polynomial. Here, t̂BRW also has the added benefit of being more
parallelizable than BRW. Their key sizes grow logarithmically in the maximum message length, except for
MHP which only requires a constant key size. Additionally, leveraging our security theorem for multivariate
polynomials, we present variants of tMMH and t̂BRW that also admit constant key size. In Sec. 4, we
describe each of these constructions in detail and analyze their security.

Benchmarking Framework. With the above choices we now have 4 × 5 distinct hash designs to com-
pare. While their security properties can be readily derived from our exposition in Sec. 4 and Thm. 4,
objectively comparing their performance is much more challenging. For this task, we build on the open-
source framework for code generation and benchmarking of Degabriele et al. [10]. Besides adding our
constituent polynomials to the framework, we also extend it to cover binary field arithmetic and multivari-
ate polynomials. The framework does not yield highly optimized implementations of the kind one would
obtain by writing directly in assembly. However, it allows us to assess the performance of different hash
designs with different parameter choices in a systematic and objective manner.

Factor Analysis. We run benchmarks for all of our two-level hash designs over a small set of parameter
choices and over varying message sizes. To make sense of this large data set and filter through it to identify
the best-performing designs, we used a statistical factor analysis, see App. E. This analysis examines the
variability in performance resulting from changes in parameter choices, exposing the parameters with the
highest weight and highest level of interaction. This step was important to validate our intuition on the
performance of the designs and to see whether there were any unexpected interactions. As we posited
earlier, we confirm that the choice of lower-level polynomial has a much higher influence on the overall
performance of the two-level construction than the higher-level one, and this becomes more pronounced
as the message length increases. Superblock size and delay parameter emerge as the two parameters with
the highest weight.

Outperforming the State of the Art. We conclude by presenting benchmarks for our best-performing
multivariate hash designs. The top-performing designs turn out to be MHP-NMH+ , t̂BRW-NMH+ and
tMMH-NMH+ , both over binary fields and prime fields. We compare these to state-of-the-art implementa-
tions such as Poly1305 implementations in OpenSSL and HACL* with AVX2, Haberdashery’s GMAC, and
Hash2L [9], as well as our implementation of d-2LHash [5] over identical prime fields.
    For binary fields, our best construction MHP-NMH+ outperforms all others by up to 25% for message
lengths exceeding 4 kB in 128-bit fields and by up to 15% past 6 kB messages in 256-bit fields, while
offering around 122 and 250 bits of security, respectively. For messages above 500 bytes, it also offers
up to 5 additional bits of security. Note that our auto-generated implementations incur overhead due to
the framework’s modularity, yet our new designs still significantly outperform state-of-the-art dedicated
implementations.
    For prime fields, a similar picture emerges. MHP-NMH+ outperforms even the highly optimized im-
plementation of Poly1305 in OpenSSL by 10%. Over the same field, it also outperforms d-2LHash by up

Intuitively the universality property is a weak form of collision resistance where the key is secret and
sampled independently of the message pair. Classically, the probability of such a collision is bounded
by a fixed parameter that depends on the maximum length of messages in the domain M. By contrast,
we employ a more fine-grained approach replacing this parameter with a function ϵ, which we refer to
as the security bound, that allows more precise bounds for different pairs of inputs. Smaller values for
the function ϵ indicate a lower collision probability and, hence, a more secure universal hash function.
Consequently, when we speak of the security of such a function, we are referring to how large (or small)
the values of ϵ can be. A stronger notion, known as ∆-universality, generalizes the universality property
further.

monomial according to this ordering evaluated at (xi )v1 = (ri )v1 . We refer to a polynomial as monic if its
leading coefficient – with respect to the chosen monomial order – is equal to 1.

3       Universality of Multivariate Polynomials
This section describes how to build a universal hash function from a multivariate polynomial over a finite
field Fq , and the security bound obtained. In particular, we quantify what security can be expected from
a polynomial with v variables. As our designs mainly consider fixed-input-length hash functions, we also
describe how to efficiently transform them into variable-input-length (VIL) hash functions in App. A.

Building Universal Hash Functions from Polynomials. Degabriele et al. [10] demonstrated that
the universality property of a hash function derived from a univariate polynomial P stems from the
injectivity and maximum degree of P . In Thm. 4, we extend this result to multivariate polynomials,
replacing the requirement on the degree of a univariate polynomial with a condition on the total degree of
a multivariate polynomial. Previous security analyses of multivariate polynomial hash functions originally
required a dedicated analysis for each specific polynomial. Thm. 4 provides sufficient conditions for a
multivariate polynomial to be a universal hash function along with its corresponding security bound.
While this bound is not always tight, injectivity is a necessary condition – without it, there exist distinct
messages whose hashes collide for every key. This result provides a novel, unified perspective on the

4    Two-Level Polynomial Hash Designs
In this section, we outline the rationale for our new universal hash designs and formally describe their
structure, along with efficient evaluation strategies. Our exploration of multivariate polynomial hashing
focuses on polynomials with a two-level structure, as illustrated in Fig. 2. Originally introduced to ac-
celerate classical univariate polynomial evaluation [23, 17], the two-level structure was later adapted in
designs combining the BRW polynomial with the classical univariate polynomial [9, 5]. Here, we extend
this framework to a broader class of polynomial instantiations – particularly multivariate constructions
– that offer improved security. As we explain below, this focus on two-level constructions is motivated
by their ability to strike a better trade-off between key length, number of multiplications, delayed limb
realignment, and parallelizability.

5     Benchmarking of New Designs
We will now discuss the performance of our new designs, starting by briefly covering important implemen-
tation aspects and our choice of reference polynomials used to evaluate performance. We then discuss our
benchmarking methodology and setup, followed by a discussion of the results, including an analysis of the
impact of various parameters on the performance of our implementations. Instructions to reproduce our
results are given in App. H.

5.1   Implementation
To implement and benchmark our designs we use the polynomial hashing framework developed by [10].
This allows for automatic generation of the field arithmetic and dynamically linking it against differ-
ent polynomial implementations, followed by testing and benchmarking. However, the framework [10]
is limited to prime fields and only has support for non-nested polynomials. We thus add support for
binary fields, message-dependent key lengths, and nesting polynomials in a modular fashion. To han-
dle message-dependent key lengths, we implement a key generator, utilizing a ChaCha20-based DRBG,
using Libsodium’s ChaCha20 implementation. As shown in App. E this is a bottleneck for our schemes
whose key size depends on the message size. Our updated version of the framework of [10] is available at
https://github.com/jangilcher/polynomial_hashing_framework.
     With these extensions we implement the polynomials from Sec. 4.1 to generate both stand-alone im-
plementations and for use as building blocks for the designs of Sec. 4.2. We parametrize our polynomial
implementations to enable testing and benchmarking of different fields using different limb realignment and
carry propagation strategies, similarly to the approach used for the classical polynomial in [10]. However,
especially for the higher-level polynomials, the adaptability of our implementations likely does not yield
peak performance. In particular, our higher-level polynomials do not currently use loop unrolling, due to
the complexity of combining this with the current generic composition approach. We do use this and other
optimizations for lower-level polynomials. Note that none of our prime field implementations make use of
vectorized instruction set extensions as these are currently unsupported by the framework of [10]. We em-
phasize that all implementations generated by the framework are full hash functions over byte strings and
so the performance and security discussions below include all the costs included in lifting our constructions
from their theoretical description in Sec. 4 to working over byte strings. This also includes always using
fresh key material and thus not amortizing internal key-generation costs over different invocations.

5.2   Reference Implementations
We compare our designs with the GMAC implementations from Haberdashery [18] and OpenSSL, Poly1305
implementations from Libsodium and OpenSSL, Poly1163 and Poly2663 from [10], as well as Hash2L [9]
and d-2LHash [5]. In addition, we also benchmarked the classical polynomial over GF(2226 − 5), GF(2128 ),
and GF(2256 ). We had to write a wrapper around the implementations of Hash2L [9] to make it fit the
methodology used in the benchmarking framework. This wrapper is not fully transparent, and is likely to
impact the measurements; see App. D for further details.
    As Hash2L is a hand-optimized implementation, we also benchmark Hash2L as generated by the frame-
work, i.e. using the framework’s field arithmetic and modular two-level implementation. This allows us to
compare designs at the same level of optimization. To disambiguate the two implementations, we call this
framework-generated version of Hash2L “Poly-BRW”, reflecting its two-level design. As [5] does not provide
an implementation of d-2LHash over GF(2116 − 3) and GF(2226 − 5), we instead use a version of d-2LHash as
generated by the framework for a like-for-like comparison. Note that [5] actually improves on these results
due to hand-optimized field arithmetic. In App. C we provide a comparison between the implementations
from [5] and the framework. Similar gains should be achievable for our generated implementations.

5.3   Benchmarking Methodology
Our approach is similar to the one chosen by [10]. We evaluate each polynomial hash function for mes-
sages of up to 16 kB in length. For each message length we collect 25 samples, each consisting of 1000
measurements. All measurements are taken with Turboboost and dynamic frequency scaling disabled us-
ing a system with an Intel Xeon Gold 6258R running at 2.7 GHz. For the Variable-Key-Length (VKL)
constructions we include the key-generation time in the benchmarks. For constructions that use a fixed
number of keys, like Hash2L, d-2LHash, and constructions using MHP at the higher level, we do not include
key-generation time.
    We instantiate our constructions over both prime and binary fields, with 100–128-bit and 200–256-bit
security levels in each case, using the following four fields: GF(2116 − 3), GF(2226 − 5), GF(2128 ), and
GF(2256 ). The choice of our prime fields is motivated by the observation in [10] that an optimal security-
performance trade-off is achieved when the limbs in the underlying field element representation are as
saturated as possible while still allowing delayed carry propagation. In particular [10] identified GF(2116 −3)
as promising candidate at the 128-bit level. For the high-security target we choose GF(2226 − 5) instead
of GF(2266 − 3), due to its increased support for delayed carry propagation while still allowing to achieve
security levels high enough for any authentication needs. When considering all possible combinations
of inner and outer polynomials from Sec. 4 including the range of possible parameters for each of the
polynomials, we are faced with a very large number of configurations to run. Thus, we run benchmarks
with reduced sampling rates only measuring for message lengths that are multiples of 100 bytes. Tabs. 4
to 6 in App. F list the security levels of all schemes considered during benchmarking.
    To better understand the design trade-offs across the many choices we perform a factor analysis on the
data obtained from our benchmarks, to estimate the contribution and importance of individual parameters.
The factor analysis and details on its methodology can be found in App. E. The factor analysis confirms our
intuitions for the performance of the two-level designs. The choice of lower-level polynomial almost always
accounts for more than half of the total variation in performance, while the higher-level only accounts for
at most 5% of the variation. The remaining variation is mostly dominated by superblock size and the
delay parameter.

5.4   Implementation Complexity and Memory Footprint
We now briefly discuss implementation complexity and memory usage. This is particularly relevant for
our two-level designs, since they use more explicit key material and precomputation than the evaluation
of the classical polynomial.
    Regarding implementation complexity, it is worth noting that efficient implementations of standard
classical polynomials are quite complex themselves [10]. High-performance implementations commonly use
two-level evaluation, precomputed powers of the hash key, delayed reductions, and other optimizations to
achieve high performance. Thus, while our multivariate polynomials are more complex at the specification
level, this gap in complexity is much less at the implementation level.
    The main memory cost in our implementations is the accumulators and key/precomputation storage.
Similarly to when implementing the classical polynomial using a two-level approach, in our designs, keys
are usually precomputed, requiring memory scaling with the superblock size for the lower-level polynomial.
Additionally, for the accumulators and keys of the higher-level polynomials, our implementations require
memory that is at most linear in the key size. In our constructions, VKL designs store accumulators
and keys that grow logarithmically with the message length, whereas in MHP, they have a fixed size.
Alternatively, for the reduced-key variants of our lower- and higher-level polynomial designs, if the memory
cost is too prohibitive and at the expense of efficiency, one can also opt to recompute the key powers
instead of storing them, thereby requiring memory storage smaller than the superblock size. For example,

Summary. Our new VKL multivariate two-level designs compete with the state-of-the-art. But their
increased security has a clear performance cost. In many cases protocol designers might prefer the increased
performance of MHP-NMH+ , which generally loses less than 10 bits of security compared to the VKL
constructions over the message size range we considered. We show that using BRW at the lower level
limits performance, and we are able to improve upon prior work [9, 5], both in terms of performance and
security, using the much simpler 1-NMH+ at the lower level instead.
     While our prime field implementations still leave room for optimization, e.g. via vectorized instruction
set extensions, we note that arithmetic in binary fields with hardware support for carryless multiplication
still massively outperforms prime fields at consistently higher security levels. As these instructions are
widely available on x86 platforms, and also increasingly on Arm processors, binary fields seem preferable.
Even when prime field implementations can be sped up significantly by using newer hardware instructions
for two independent carry chains as in [9, 5], the benefits gained from the choice of prime fields over
binary fields seem small, since (as far as we know) carryless multiplication is also always available on these
platforms.

parallel with the encryption component while the other is inherently sequential and must be evaluated

6    Conclusion
In this paper, we explored the design space of multivariate polynomial UHFs via a two-level approach
inspired by [9, 5]. Extending the code-generation and benchmarking framework of [10], and complementing
it with a factor analysis, we identified attractive lower- and higher-level polynomial combinations, yielding
new UHF designs whose performance matches or surpasses the state of the art in leading cryptographic
libraries and the implementations of [9]. We highlight two complementary designs: MHP-NMH+ , which
delivers very high performance and improved security over the state of the art for all but very short
messages; and tMMH-NMH+ , which, for any given field, attains the highest security – with minimal
loss as message length increases – at state-of-the-art speed. Both meet our three goals from Sec. 1:
short keys, reduced multiplication complexity, and compatibility with delayed-operation optimizations
and parallelizability. Despite relying on auto-generated code, our designs remain competitive, whereas
prior benchmarks used carefully optimized assembly code. Given its higher security due to a larger
field, d-2LHash1271 [5] is also an attractive option for a 128-bit prime-field hash. A general finding is
that binary fields typically outperform prime fields at similar security levels, largely due to carryless-
multiply instructions. Considering NIST’s current standardization efforts for a 256-bit block cipher and
new AEAD/Accordion modes, use of MHP-NMH+ could lead to performance increases between 5 and 26%,
depending on field size and AEAD construction.
    Our results point to designs worth further optimization; based on prior hand-optimized work [17, 6, 5,
18], we expect significant additional speedups. Further gains should accrue from vectorized instruction-set
extensions that compute several superblocks in parallel. Automating code generation to exploit these
features across a wide range of UHF designs remains an important open problem.

D                       Benchmarking Methodology for Hash2L and d-2LHash
For Hash2L we observed that for the original benchmarks in [9], the hash function interface requires that
the message and key inputs are already stored in 128-bit SSE registers used by Intel’s carryless multiplica-
tion instruction. However, the benchmarks in [9] only seem to measure the hash function execution time,
excluding any overhead of transforming byte strings into the concrete representation used in the imple-
mentation. This is incompatible with the benchmarking framework of [10]. But, as we argue, it is also
unrealistic, as the memory operations involved in these transforms can be very costly and have to be done
in any real world implementation. Our wrappers – and thus our benchmarks – for Hash2L include these
memory operations. This leads to noticeable increase in running time compared to the results originally
reported in [9].
    For d-2LHash we also observed issues related to memory usage. Specifically, the implementation of [5]
requires that the message is stored in a buffer of at least 8 KiB (plus a few bytes depending on the
exact variant). Otherwise, the implementation performs out-of-bounds memory accesses leading to stack
overflows and segmentation faults. Thus, our wrappers first copy the message into a new buffer of sufficient
size. The cost of these copies is again included in our benchmarks. As the memory layout itself is simple
and contiguous these copies are rather fast and our measurements are similar to those reported in [5]. As
d-2LHash has several parameters that affect performance, and the configuration that worked best on the
machines used in [5] might not be the best for our CPU, we benchmark all variants provided in [5] and
compare our designs against the variants performing the best. To be consistent with our implementations
we include time spent on key precomputation when benchmarking d-2LHash.
    We also note that for both Hash2L and d-2LHash, the respective benchmarking scripts have a hard-coded

limit of 8 KiB for the message size. Our benchmarks generally measure for messages up to 16 kB. While
the implementations seem to work for messages past 8 KiB, we did not perform any further correctness
tests on them.

VKL Polynomials. Figure 15 shows the percentage of variation explained by the different factors
for the four different fields at different message sizes for the models including key-generation time and
Fig. 16. shows the same for the models excluding key-generation time. We observe that as message length
increases the impact of the choice of lower-level polynomial quickly rises, becoming the dominant factor in
all fields except the smaller prime field. This is consistent with our expectations as, asymptotically, most
of the computation happens at the leaves of the tree construction where the evaluation of the lower-level
polynomial takes place. This effect is more pronounced both for binary fields and larger fields and is caused
by the different performance characteristics of the hardware instructions used for the field arithmetic, and
the need to handle carries for prime fields. The absence of carry bits in binary fields allows us to always
fully delay the reduction in the lower-level polynomial. Thus, the delay parameter simply controls the
loop unrolling factor and so its relative impact is reduced. This effect is furthermore compounded by the
higher contention on the CPU’s execution units used for binary field arithmetic when compared to prime
field arithmetic. This significantly reduces the impact of loop unrolling, further decreasing the impact
of the delay parameter for binary fields. In addition, a larger field size allows for a larger blocksize thus
requiring less field operations per message. For prime fields this effect also reduces the impact of using
delayed reduction, as reductions generally happen less frequently. On the other hand, smaller fields also
increase the effect of good pipeline utilization via loop unrolling, as a single field operation consists of
fewer dependent instructions. However, to make use of this at the lower level, the message superblocks
have to be large enough to be able to fully exploit the pipelines during the lower level computations.
Furthermore, the superblock size has a significant impact for smaller messages due to its effect on the cost
of key generation. More specifically, it directly dictates the number of keys required for a message of a
fixed size.

H.1     Abstract
The artifact accompanying this paper contains the source code of our updated polynomial hashing frame-
work, together with the configuration files needed to reproduce the main performance results, described
in Sec. 5.5, for the new universal hash functions over binary fields. It also includes the source code and
benchmark scripts for the Rijndael256-based AEAD schemes from Sec. 5.6.
    We further include docker compose configuration files to easily set up all dependencies. The provided
scripts generate, compile, test, and benchmark the relevant implementations, and produce the benchmark
data and plots used to validate the paper’s main performance claims. Beyond reproducing the reported
experiments, the framework is intended to be reusable: researchers can select different field options, bench-
mark additional parameter choices, and add new polynomial constructions or reference implementations.

noted in the respective files.

We recommend using a Linux system and configuring the system to run the CPU at a fixed frequency. This

scaling using cpufrequtils package, which can usually be found in most Linux distribution’s package
repositories. On Ubuntu, it can be installed with:
sudo apt install cpufrequtils
We recommend setting the frequency to the base frequency of the CPU. On our system (Intel Xeon Gold

privileges:
cores=$(cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep processor | awk ’{print␣$3}’)
for i in $cores;
    do
        cpufreq-set -c $i -g performance;
        cpufreq-set -c $i -d 2.7GHz;
        cpufreq-set -c $i -u 2.7GHz;

H.4.1    Major claims
Note that our artifacts only relate to our performance claims, as such the major claims in this section only

(C1): 1-MHP-1-NMH+ outperforms the state-of-the-art (Hash2L) by up to 25% in the 128-bit case and up

(C2): The performance impact of increasing the number of keys for MHP-NMH+ over binary fields from 1

     whose results are depicted in Fig. 8 and discussed in Sec. 5.5.
(C3): For 128-bit fields the VKL constructions, t̂BRW-NMH+ and tMMH-NMH+ , achieve performance

     in Sec. 5.3, whose results are depicted in Fig. 8 and discussed in Sec. 5.5.
(C4): The use of MHP-NMH+ in a 256-bit blocksize Rijndael-based AEAD scheme leads to large perfor-
     mance improvements over using the classical polynomial (about 5% for 128-bit authenticators and
     21% for 256-bit authenticators). This is shown by our benchmarking (E3) described in Sec. 5.6,
